implementation_notes: The BCL keeps the size/capacity split visible: List<T> has Count and Capacity, and TrimExcess() 'sets the capacity to the actual number of elements ... if that number is less than a threshold value' - the Remarks add that it does nothing once the list is above 90% of capacity (a threshold that may change), deliberately declining to pay a reallocation for a small gain. Assign Capacity = Count when the reallocation must happen instead; Queue<T>, Stack<T> and HashSet<T> expose TrimExcess() with the same shape, and StringBuilder trims through its settable Capacity (sb.Capacity = sb.Length). Arrays have no capacity layer at all, so their equivalent is the copy: Array.Resize(ref arr, n) allocates a right-sized array and copies the live range.
pitfalls: TrimExcess() is documented as doing nothing when the list is more than 90% of capacity (and the threshold may change in future releases), so it is a heuristic, not a guarantee - set Capacity = Count when the shrink must happen.

Capacity = Count throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException if the value is below Count, and the reallocation copies the whole list (O(n)): trim after the filtering phase, not inside the filter, and never on a hot path.

The reallocation replaces the backing array under anyone holding a view of it: a Span<T>/Memory<T> or CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan slice obtained earlier goes stale, and List<T> is not synchronized, so a concurrent reader can observe the swap.
sources: learn.microsoft.com, List<T>.TrimExcess() - 'Sets the capacity to the actual number of elements in the List<T>, if that number is less than a threshold value'; Remarks: 'the TrimExcess method does nothing if the list is at more than 90 percent of capacity ... The current threshold of 90 percent might change in future releases'; 'This method is an O(n) operation': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1.trimexcess
